detail.extracted_title: Botanical Wraps and Circular Ventures: Inside the University of Nizwa's Biodegradable Food Films and Oman's Green Accelerator
detail.excerpt: Researchers in Nizwa have engineered edible, antimicrobial food packaging from seaweed biopolymers and essential oils—just as be'ah opens the fourth cohort of Eco-Innovate Oman to scale circular-economy startups.
detail.article_html:
In the Sustainable Packaging Laboratory at the University of Nizwa, a thin, translucent sheet rests on a glass tray under the analytical balance. It looks and flexes much like ordinary kitchen cling wrap, yet it contains not a single drop of petroleum plastic. Compounded from sodium alginate extracted from brown seaweed, chitosan, and natural Omani aromatic essential oils, the film is completely edible, biodegradable, and actively slows bacterial spoilage on fresh produce.

On the exact same day that the University of Nizwa published the findings of this biopolymer breakthrough, Oman Environmental Services Holding Company (be'ah) announced the opening of applications for the fourth cohort of Eco-Innovate Oman, the country's dedicated circular-economy accelerator for small and medium enterprises. Viewed together, the two announcements capture a practical shift taking root across Oman's environmental sector: sustainability is moving out of conference halls and into wet-chemistry laboratories and commercial startup incubators.

Turning Seaweed Polymers and Essential Oils into Active Packaging

Across the global food industry, single-use synthetic plastic films remain one of the hardest waste streams to replace. Conventional polyethylene wraps keep moisture in, yet they persist in landfills and marine ecosystems for decades and offer zero active protection against microbial oxidation on the surface of fresh fruit, meat, or dairy.

To address both problems at once, Dr. Saurabh Bhatia, Associate Professor in the Sustainable Packaging Laboratory at the University of Nizwa, partnered with Dr. Ahmed bin Mohammed Al Harrasi, Vice Chancellor for Graduate Studies, Research and External Relations and Director of the Natural and Medical Sciences Research Center, alongside Dr. Ahmed Al Hadhrami from the Department of Biological and Chemical Sciences. Funded jointly by the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Water Resources and the Authority for Scientific Research and Innovation under the Strategic Research Projects Program, the team engineered composite biodegradable films using sodium alginate and chitosan reinforced with natural aromatic essential oils.

Every base ingredient in the formulation holds Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) status for human consumption. When the researchers tested the composite sheets against standard biopolymer films, the addition of essential oils did far more than impart a clean botanical aroma. The essential oils locked into the polymer matrix significantly boosted antioxidant and antimicrobial resistance, increased the film's tensile elasticity, and reduced water-vapor permeability—creating a breathable yet protective skin that slows oxidation and extends the shelf life of perishable foods.

The team's experimental findings were peer-reviewed and published across three leading international journals in 2024—the International Journal of Biological Macromolecules, Food & Function, and the Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture—and the laboratory is now preparing pilot-scale trials with Omani food processing companies to test how the films perform on commercial packaging lines.

Eco-Innovate Oman Opens Its Fourth Circular-Economy Cohort

That transition from laboratory validation to commercial production is precisely where Oman's circular-economy infrastructure comes into play. Since launching in 2019 as the Sultanate's first specialized environmental incubator, Eco-Innovate Oman—run by be'ah—has focused on helping Omani entrepreneurs turn waste-diversion, resource-recovery, and clean-material concepts into viable businesses.

As Dr. Mohab bin Ali Al Hinai, Vice President for Sustainability and Circular Economy at be'ah, noted when opening registration for the fourth cohort (which runs through December 10), early-stage environmental startups rarely fail for lack of scientific imagination; they fail when they lack regulatory guidance, industrial testing partners, and investor-ready unit economics.

To bridge those different stages of company maturity, the fourth edition of Eco-Innovate Oman splits into two distinct tracks: an Incubation Track designed for early-stage founders validating circular-economy prototypes, and an Acceleration Track tailored for established small and medium enterprises ready to scale up manufacturing, integrate Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) standards, and expand into regional markets.

Whether an Omani venture is compounding essential-oil food wraps in a Nizwa university lab or designing closed-loop industrial recycling systems in Muscat, the underlying direction is the same: building domestic materials and companies that replace imported waste with homegrown value.

detail.instagram_caption:
Inside the Sustainable Packaging Laboratory at the University of Nizwa, researchers have developed an edible, biodegradable alternative to petroleum-based plastic food wrap using sodium alginate, chitosan, and natural aromatic essential oils.

Led by Dr. Saurabh Bhatia alongside Dr. Ahmed bin Mohammed Al Harrasi and Dr. Ahmed Al Hadhrami—and co-funded by the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Water Resources and the Authority for Scientific Research and Innovation—the research demonstrates that embedding natural essential oils into GRAS-certified biopolymers strengthens film elasticity, blocks moisture loss, and actively inhibits oxidation and microbial growth on perishable food. Published across three international scientific journals, the project is now moving toward industrial trials with local food producers.

That push from lab bench to market aligns directly with the launch of the fourth cohort of Eco-Innovate Oman by be'ah, which opened registration through December 10 with dedicated Incubation and Acceleration tracks to help Omani circular-economy startups and SMEs commercialize sustainable materials and resource-recovery solutions.
